手順・やり方.quote: How to Estimate Private Company Revenue for M&A | Nodior

To estimate a private company's revenue, collect several independent public signals of its size: headcount from job ads, staff pages and benefit-plan filings, plus licenses, permits, fleet and locations. Multiply headcount by a revenue-per-employee band typical for the industry, check it against a second method such as payroll, and report a range with a confidence level.
To turn signals into dollars, use two methods that rely on different inputs, and let the range cover both.
Run it from the lower of the two low ends to the higher of the two high ends. If the methods don't overlap at all, the headcount or a band is wrong. Find out which before you report anything.
Several independent signals agree, and the two methods give ranges that overlap.
The company, signals and bands are made up to show the method. Real bands vary by region and service mix.

The low end comes from the payroll method and the high end from the headcount method. Four independent signals agree on about 50 people with a fleet to match, the methods overlap, and the one signal that disagrees has a known cause.
For a handful of companies, you can do this yourself with the steps above. None of the data is secret. It takes time to find, date and cross-check.

It's a good starting point, but public headcounts are often wrong for field-heavy companies, and the right band depends on the service mix. Check it against a second method, such as payroll, permit volume or fleet size.

実例.quote: Worked example: a commercial HVAC company
The example is a commercial HVAC contractor serving two counties in one metro area, with service contracts, repairs and equipment replacement.

Public companies report revenue every quarter. Private companies in the US have no such duty. State annual reports name officers and a registered agent, rarely revenue, and tax filings stay confidential.

Use at least two sources that don't depend on each other. A benefit-plan filing and a job ad are independent. A staff page and a profile copied from it count once. Decide whether regular subcontractors are in the count.
Two signals agree, or one strong signal carries the estimate, such as a recent benefit-plan filing.

The benefit-plan filing and the job ads are independent and agree, so the profile count is set aside and the gap is noted next to the estimate.
A three-year-old filing or a job ad posted before a branch closed describes a different company.

Multiply headcount by a revenue-per-employee band typical for the industry, check it against a second method such as payroll, and report a range with a confidence level.

For a payroll-based check, estimate payroll from headcount and public wage data for the trade and region. Then divide by the share of revenue that payroll usually takes in that kind of business. Permit volume or fleet size can add a further check.
Revenue is always a range, and these estimates are not audited financials. They tell you which companies are likely the right size, so you can rank targets before anyone calls an owner.

Estimated revenue: $6 million to $9 million, high confidence.
Owner-led companies often rely on subcontractors and family members. Leaving them out makes a headcount-based estimate come in low.

How accurate is a private company revenue estimate?

It depends on how many independent signals agree, which is why each estimate carries a confidence level. A low-confidence range is a starting point for your own questions to the owner. None of these estimates are audited financials.
Can you estimate revenue for a company with almost no online presence?

Often, yes. Licenses, permits, vehicle registrations and benefit-plan filings exist whether or not a company markets itself. When the record is thin, we mark the estimate low confidence instead of guessing.
